overview: Utahraptor ostrommaysorum was the largest dromaeosaurid theropod known, reaching 5–7 metres and weighing an estimated 300–500 kg. From the early Early Cretaceous Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah (~126 Ma), its discovery in 1991 — announced just as Jurassic Park was in production — provided real-world justification for the large "Velociraptors" depicted in the film.

A remarkable Utahraptor bonebed in the Doelling's Bowl area of Utah preserves multiple individuals, including young, trapped in a quicksand-like deposit together. Whether this represents pack behaviour — the animals dying while hunting together — or independent individuals drawn to a prey carcass and individually becoming mired is debated, but the multi-individual deposit is one of the most significant large theropod bonebeds from the Early Cretaceous.

articles.title: Discovery and the Jurassic Park connection
articles.body: James Kirkland, Robert Gaston and Donald Burge described Utahraptor in 1993. The announcement came while Jurassic Park was in post-production; producer Steven Spielberg reportedly offered money to support the research after realising the timing and the significance. The film's oversized Velociraptors were — somewhat accidentally — a reasonable approximation of Utahraptor in scale.

articles.title: The sickle claw
articles.body: The enlarged sickle claw of Utahraptor is proportionally massive — up to 24 cm long on the foot — and considerably larger in absolute terms than that of Deinonychus or Velociraptor. Functional analysis suggests it was used to pin and puncture large prey rather than slash: the claw shape is optimised for penetration, not cutting.

articles.title: Bonebed and social behaviour
articles.body: The Doelling's Bowl bonebed — fully described in 2023 — preserves at least 6 individuals in different growth stages entombed in what was likely a sand blow or quicksand deposit. The assemblage includes an adult, several sub-adults and juveniles. The age range is consistent with a family group or social unit, but catastrophic individual trapping cannot be excluded. This is the most important multi-individual large dromaeosaurid site known.

record.description: Utahraptor ostrommaysorum was a giant dromaeosaurid from the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, known from several incomplete individuals and a difficult multi-individual block.
facts: Large sickle claws and robust limb elements are directly known.
New dating places the Stikes Quarry near 135.1 Ma, in the Valanginian rather than the Barremian; the 280 kg point mass is cleared as too precise.

presentation.heroLead: The largest known dromaeosaurid, a giant sickle-clawed predator from Early Cretaceous Utah that is famous out of proportion to its fossils: a handful of bones and a nine-tonne block of sandstone still being prepared.

heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Fred Wierum. The feathered covering is inferred from smaller dromaeosaurids that preserve feathers; body proportions are partly modelled on relatives because no complete skeleton is known.

animalParagraphs: Utahraptor was a heavily built dromaeosaurid, the family of sickle-clawed predators that includes Velociraptor and Deinonychus, from the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in eastern Utah. It was named in 1993 from a huge foot claw and a few other bones found near Moab, and remains by far the largest member of its family.

The known bones show an animal several times heavier than Deinonychus, with a robust, deep-snouted premaxilla, thick limb bones and a curved second-toe claw whose bony core alone is over 20 centimetres long. Published lengths of five to seven metres and masses from about 280 to 500 kilograms or more are estimates scaled from relatives, not measurements of a complete skeleton.

In 2001 a sandstone block from Utahraptor Ridge, later dated to about 135 million years ago, was found to contain the remains of several Utahraptor individuals of different sizes together with an iguanodontian. Its slow preparation promises a far better picture of the animal, but most of that material is not yet published.
animalHighlights: The bony core of the second-toe claw is over 20 cm long, the largest known for any dromaeosaurid.
Thick, robust limb bones and a deep premaxilla indicate a heavy animal rather than a scaled-up Velociraptor.
A multi-individual block from Utahraptor Ridge includes juveniles, but is still being prepared.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Serrated teeth in the premaxilla and the enlarged sickle claw indicate a predator. No bite-marked prey or gut contents are documented.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.level: Inferred from limb bones and relatives
lifeCards.reason: Hindlimb elements match the two-legged plan of other dromaeosaurids. Running speed and any pack hunting are not evidenced.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: No complete adult is known. Lengths and masses come from scaling claws, limb bones and the premaxilla against smaller relatives.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Utahraptor preserves no feathers or skin; the feathered look follows Microraptor and other dromaeosaurids that do.

presentation.classificationSummary: Utahraptor is a dromaeosaurid, usually placed in Dromaeosaurinae alongside Dromaeosaurus and the Mongolian Achillobator. Its exact position depends on which of its fragmentary bones are scored, and it may move once the block material is described.

questions.title: How big was a full-grown adult?
questions.copy: Estimates of 5–7 m and 280–500 kg or more rest on isolated bones. The largest elements in the block may revise both figures.

questions.title: Did it hunt in packs?
questions.copy: Several individuals occur together in the Utahraptor Ridge block, but they may have been trapped in a quicksand-like deposit rather than hunting together. Pack behaviour is not demonstrated.

questions.title: Which bones belong to which animal?
questions.copy: The holotype claw, the paratypes and the block specimens come from different sites and individuals. Until the block is fully prepared, the association of many elements is uncertain.

review.ageReviewNote: CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb dating and carbon-isotope stratigraphy place the Utahraptor Ridge horizon at 135.10 +/- 0.30 Ma, in the Valanginian.

panel.headline: A giant foot claw, a few associated bones and a block full of unprepared skeletons.
panel.standfirst: Utahraptor ostrommaysorum was named from a large pedal ungual and a small set of paratype bones from the Gaston Quarry. A sandstone block from Utahraptor Ridge containing multiple individuals has been under preparation since 2014 and remains largely unpublished.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: Skull, limb and claw elements are known from several fragmentary individuals, but no articulated or near-complete skeleton has been described, and much of the vertebral column and girdles are documented only from unprepared block material.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype pedal ungual; paratype bones including a premaxilla, a lacrimal, a tibia and a large manual ungual; and a growing collection of skull and postcranial elements from the Utahraptor Ridge block, which contains several individuals of different sizes.
knownRemains.note: Most of what is written about the shape of Utahraptor comes from scaling these pieces against Deinonychus and other relatives. Formal description of the block material is still awaited.

media.title: Sickle claw attributed to Utahraptor
media.alt: A large curved pedal ungual attributed to Utahraptor on display at the BYU Museum of Paleontology
media.caption: A large sickle claw attributed to Utahraptor on display at the Brigham Young University Museum of Paleontology. The holotype claw, CEU 184v.86, is held at the Prehistoric Museum in Price, Utah; keratin would have extended the claw well beyond the bone shown.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A deep premaxilla with teeth and a lacrimal among the paratypes; further skull elements reported from the block.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Only partially documented; vertebrae are present in the block but not yet fully described.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: A tibia, the large second-toe ungual of the holotype and a manual ungual, plus additional limb bones from the block.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No feathers, skin or gut contents are known.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A giant sickle claw, a deep toothed premaxilla, a tibia and other bones from several fragmentary individuals, plus block material in preparation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A robust, exceptionally large dromaeosaurine predator, the heaviest known member of its family.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Adult size and mass, most of the skull and vertebral column, whether the block individuals died together by chance, and the presence of feathers.
